title: Complexity
summary: Bound time and space, and say when the question wants amortized cost.

parts.rule: Bound time and space with big-O that names the dominant term. Say when the question wants amortized cost instead of a single-call worst case.
parts.why: Without a bound, two solutions that both "work on the sample" are incomparable. Interviewers ask for the bound to see whether you notice nested loops, hidden copies, or a clever structure that removes a factor.
parts.example: SAMPLE: a double loop over n elements with constant work inside is Θ(n²) time and Θ(1) extra space. A hash-map frequency pass then a single walk is expected Θ(n) time and Θ(k) space for k distinct keys. You state both pairs, not only the happy path.
parts.use: Lead with complexity when comparing approaches, when sizing a phone-screen solution, or when an amortized structure like a dynamic array is in play. Clarify best, average, and worst if the prompt hinges on adversarial input.

body:
Rule. Bound time and space with big-O that names the dominant term. Say when the question wants amortized cost instead of a single-call worst case.

Why it matters. Without a bound, two solutions that both "work on the sample" are incomparable. Interviewers ask for the bound to see whether you notice nested loops, hidden copies, or a clever structure that removes a factor.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: a double loop over n elements with constant work inside is Θ(n²) time and Θ(1) extra space. A hash-map frequency pass then a single walk is expected Θ(n) time and Θ(k) space for k distinct keys. You state both pairs, not only the happy path.

When to use. Lead with complexity when comparing approaches, when sizing a phone-screen solution, or when an amortized structure like a dynamic array is in play. Clarify best, average, and worst if the prompt hinges on adversarial input.

When to refuse. Refuse quoting a bound you cannot justify from the code shape. Refuse ignoring space when the map or recursion depth is the real limit. Refuse mixing amortized append with a claim that every append is worst-case constant.
